r: Destination Development trains students to plan, manage, and promote recreation and tourism destinations, integrating sustainability principles into destination marketing, planning, and policy across urban, public, private, and volunteer settings. These tasks map onto O*NET activities such as analyzing data or information, developing objectives and strategies, and communicating with persons outside the organization, categories where observed-usage data already shows AI prominent in office and marketing work. Much of the course's promotional and planning-document output, including destination marketing copy, market analysis, and policy summaries, is highly exposed, since AI already drafts comparable material competently. The general_studies_designation field is empty, so no gen-ed transfer mandate protects the course, and no clinical or licensure hold applies to this hospitality curriculum. At 24 months, however, diffusion into destination-management agencies remains limited and planning still requires synthesizing local economic and policy context, so realized automatability stays partial. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly perform much of the analytical and promotional work destination planners rely on, including market segmentation, sustainability-integrated marketing copy, policy briefs, and economic-impact framing, echoing the productivity gains professional writing has shown in controlled studies of AI-assisted drafting. Task-exposure research classifies marketing and planning-adjacent writing among the most automatable knowledge-work categories, and destination promotion sits squarely there. No embodiment protects this course, since its work is digital analysis and communication rather than fieldwork, and its F3 rating stays high across horizons. With general_studies_designation empty and no accreditation credit-hour floor specific to hospitality destination courses, no institutional cap holds the rating down. The residual, synthesizing local stakeholder interests, sustainability trade-offs, and cross-jurisdictional policy nuance, still needs a human, but forms a shrinking share of the course's applied content as tools mature. Rating rises to High.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most routine destination-marketing and planning-document work, including drafting promotional strategy, running economic and visitor-impact analysis, and synthesizing sustainability policy across jurisdictions, competently and with limited human input, consistent with the capability trend of rapidly widening task-time horizons documented in recent forecasting work. Destination Development carries no foundational-scaffolding role that would cap the rating, since it is not prerequisite substrate for other required coursework, and no institutional or licensure lock applies, given the empty general_studies_designation field and the absence of a hospitality accreditation mandate tied to this specific course. The instrumental case for taking this exact course to acquire these skills is substantially eroded. The genuine hedge is that destination development involves reconciling public, private, and volunteer-agency interests in particular places, a stakeholder-negotiation residue that could sustain more human involvement than a pure capability read implies, and ten-year forecasts carry wide uncertainty. Rating remains High.
RTM 4000.d: This course prepares students for successfully planning, managing, and promoting sustainable recreation and tourism destinations. The course delves into integrating sustainability principles in destination management, marketing, and planning across diverse settings, such as urban, public, private, and volunteer agencies. Students will also explore contemporary issues related to economics and policy in both local and global contexts within the recreation and tourism industry. Recreation Professions
